facts.claim: "I'm So Good At Being Alone" is the seventh and closing track on Knox's seven-track EP "I'm So Good At Being Alone?", released October 6, 2023.
The EP's copyright line reads Barbershop Records under exclusive license to Atlantic Recording Corporation.
The title track was co-written by DCF and co-written and produced by Captain Cuts.
Deezer's writer credits for the track are Ben Berger, David Charles Fisher, Knox Morris and Ryan Rabin.

Euphoria describes the EP title as a question and the title track as a statement, which it reads as a phase of personal reconciliation. It places the song at the end of an arc running from "Man Down" through "Love Letter" to moving on.
Knox told Euphoria that his first record was about losing someone and that this one is the process of getting over that.
Knox said the title song expands on what he and his team were capable of, and that the EP sounds more mature than his first EP, How to Lose a Girl in 7 Songs.
The EP includes the singles "Not The 1975" and "We're Not In Love Anymore" (feat. Charlotte Sands). Nightly features on "Miss When You Missed Me".
Knox's first EP, How to Lose a Girl in 7 Songs, came out February 17, 2023. It includes the viral 2022 single "Sneakers".
Knox Morris grew up in Dayton, Ohio, and attended Ohio University planning to become a teacher. He dropped out and moved to Nashville in early 2019. He later signed to Atlantic Records.

research.lineage: Knox's music sits in the Nashville-based, social-media-driven indie-pop and pop-rock scene, with AllMusic comparing it to the folk-pop of Ed Sheeran and the indie rock of The Band Camino.

draft:
The punctuation tells half the story. Knox titled his 2023 EP *I'm So Good At Being Alone?*, question mark and all, then closed it with **I'm So Good At Being Alone**, no question mark. Euphoria read that gap as the record's arc: a question the earlier songs ask, a statement the last one finally makes. Knox told the magazine his first record was about losing someone and this one is the process of getting over that. The title track is where he lands, or at least where he says he does.

The first verse sells the perks with a straight face. He wakes whenever he wants, takes both sides of the bed, and skips a party for video games. It's light and a little goofy, and it's honest too, because that small freedom after a breakup is real. But the lyric keeps leaving its own door open. In the second verse he admits "I won't feel like this forever," then decides to enjoy it while it lasts. That sounds like someone who knows the good mood is borrowed. Then comes "I swear it's not that bad." People don't swear about things that don't need defending.

The section before the last chorus is where the two feelings sit right on top of each other. "There's no one here but I'm not lonely, not lonely," he sings, and every line there doubles its final words, like a person saying something twice to hear whether it holds. He's done crying, he insists. Maybe. The song never settles whether this is healing or a pep talk, and it's better for leaving both in the room.

The sound picks the pep talk. A four-on-the-floor kick drives everything, with hi-hats ticking over a simple, repeating bass line. A synth pad holds underneath while a clean, arpeggiated guitar figure spins on top. It's moderately fast, bright and polished, with enough reverb on the voice and drums to give it room. Knox sings it clear and confident, a little detached, the way you'd tell your friends you're fine. That cool delivery gives him away. The track is dancing while the voice holds something at arm's length.

Knox dropped out of Ohio University, where he'd planned to become a teacher, and moved to Nashville in 2019. He wrote this song with David Charles Fisher, Ben Berger and Ryan Rabin, and Captain Cuts produced it. It comes out of the Nashville, social-media-driven pop-rock scene that AllMusic ties to the Band Camino and Ed Sheeran. Knox said the song expands on what he and his team were capable of, and the bounce under such a shaky claim backs him up.

It sticks because you can dance to it and doubt it at the same time, and that's what most people getting over someone are doing anyway.
